text: نظرت جدتي من النافذة طويلاً وهي تنتظر عودة أبي من السوق.
translation: My grandmother watched from the window for a long time, waiting for my father to get back from the market.

text: قدّمت الآنسةُ ريم استقالتها بعد شهرين فقط من تعيينها في القسم.
translation: Miss Reem handed in her resignation only two months after she was appointed to the department.

text: كتبتُ اسمي على علبة الطعام حتى لا يأخذها أحد من الثلاجة.
translation: I wrote my name on the food container so nobody would take it from the fridge.

text: يدرّس مارك اللغة الإنجليزية في معهد وسط المدينة منذ ثلاث سنوات.
translation: Mark has been teaching English at an institute downtown for three years.

text: قف مكاني في الطابور دقيقتين حتى أشتري الخبز من الفرن.
translation: Hold my place in the queue for two minutes while I get bread from the bakery.

text: نام الطفل على وسادة عالية، فاشتكى من ألم في عنقه صباحاً.
translation: The boy slept on a high pillow and complained of a pain in his neck in the morning.

text: شدّ المحاضر ربطة عنقه قبل أن يدخل قاعة المؤتمر المزدحمة.
translation: The lecturer tightened his necktie before walking into the packed conference hall.

text: يتقاضى العمال في السوق أجرهم اليومي مساءً قبل إغلاق المحال.
translation: The labourers in the market collect their daily wage in the evening, before the shops close.

text: ملأت رائحة الجيف الطريق الترابي، فأغلقنا نوافذ السيارة بسرعة.
translation: The stench of the carcasses filled the dirt road, so we quickly shut the car windows.

text: غيرت الشركة سياسة الإجازات، فصار على الموظف أن يطلبها قبل شهر.
translation: The company changed its leave policy, so an employee now has to request time off a month ahead.

text: المدينة تغيرت كثيرًا، ولم تعد كما تركتها قبل عشر سنوات.
translation: The city has changed a great deal; it is no longer as I left it ten years ago.

text: أشعر أنّي خارج الحكاية كلّما تحدّث أصدقائي عن سنوات الجامعة.
translation: I feel like I'm outside the story whenever my friends talk about their university years.

text: تخبز أمي الخبز كل جمعة، فتملأ رائحته البيت والدرج معاً.
translation: My mother bakes bread every Friday, and the smell fills the flat and the stairwell alike.

text: آمل أن يتوقف المطر قبل الغروب حتى ننشر الغسيل على السطح.
translation: I hope the rain stops before sunset so we can hang the washing out on the roof.

text: من يقدر على حمل هذه الصناديق وحده يستحق أجرا مضاعفا.
translation: Anyone who can carry these crates on his own deserves double pay.

text: بدا الامتحان سهلا في أوله، ثم جاء السؤال الأخير وأربك الجميع.
translation: The exam seemed easy at the start, and then the last question came and threw everyone.

text: يعمل خالي مهندسًا على سفينة شحن تنقل الحبوب بين جدة وجيبوتي.
translation: My uncle works as an engineer on a cargo ship that carries grain between Jeddah and Djibouti.

text: كل تفصيل في تلك الليلة ما زال محفورا في ذاكرتي.
translation: Every detail of that night is still carved into my memory.

text: ما زال أهل الحي يتحدثون عن فعلة الجار الذي أطفأ الحريق بمفرده.
translation: People in the neighbourhood still talk about what the neighbour did when he put out the fire single-handed.

text: Arabic has one subject pronoun per person, and in the singular both the second and the third person split by gender.  | Person | Pronoun | | --- | --- | | I | أنا | | you, masculine | أنتَ | | you, feminine | أنتِ | | he | هو | | she | هي | | we | نحن | | you, plural | أنتم | | they | هم |  The two singular 'you' forms are the same three letters — only the final vowel differs, anta to a man and anti to a woman — so unvowelled both are written أنت, and the sentence has to say which is meant.
Arabic drops 'to be' in the present: البيت كبير (the house [is] big), أنا سعيد (I [am] happy). Subject + predicate, nothing in between — a complete, correct sentence.

**ال** attaches to the noun: بيت (a house) → البيت (the house).  Before 'sun letters' (ت، د، س، ش، ص، ن…) the ل assimilates in speech: الشارع sounds ash-shāriʿ, not al-shāriʿ. Before 'moon letters' (ب، ك، م، ق…) the ل is pronounced: القمر = al-qamar.  Writing never changes — only the sound.

text: Nouns are masculine or feminine; the letter ة at the end usually marks feminine: معلم (male teacher) → معلمة (female teacher), طالب → طالبة.  Most profession and role words come in this pair.

| Pointing | Masculine | Feminine | | --- | --- | --- | | this, near | هذا | هذه | | that, far | ذلك | تلك |  هذه is also the form used with the ة words. With an indefinite noun a demonstrative makes a whole sentence: هذا كتاب (this is a book); with a definite noun it points inside a phrase: هذا الكتاب (this book…), ذلك الكتاب (that book), تلك المدينة (that city).

The adjective FOLLOWS the noun and matches it, feature by feature:  - gender: سيارة جديدة (a new car), the ة on both words - definiteness: بيت كبير (a big house), البيت الكبير (the big house) — ال on both or on neither - case: أقرأ كتاباً جديداً (I am reading a new book), the accusative ending on both  Two words, matching uniforms.

Most Arabic words grow from a three-consonant root poured into patterns.  From ك-ت-ب (writing): كتاب (book), كاتب (writer — the 'doer' pattern), مكتب (office/desk — the 'place' pattern), مكتبة (library).  Learn to spot the root and unknown words start explaining themselves.

Two nouns side by side make 'the X of Y': كتاب الطالب (the student's book), باب البيت (the door of the house). The FIRST noun never takes ال — definiteness comes from the second.  No word for 'of' at all.

Possessives attach to the noun, one suffix per owner:  | Owner | Suffix | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | my | ي | كتابي | | your, masculine | ك | كتابك | | his | ه | كتابه | | her | ها | كتابها | | our | نا | كتابنا |  Feminine ة opens into ت before the suffix: سيارة → سيارتي (my car).  The pattern is iḍāfa again — with a pronoun as the owner.
The present conjugates with prefixes: أ (I) — أدرس (I study), ت (you/she) — تدرس, ي (he) — يدرس, ن (we) — ندرس.  'They' adds an ending too: يدرسون. Prefix first, root inside.

Two negators cover the present, one for each sentence type: لا goes before a present-tense verb (لا أفهم — I don't understand), and ليس negates a nominal sentence (هو ليس هنا — he is not here). ليس is itself a verb and conjugates:  | Person | Form | | --- | --- | | I | لستُ | | he | ليس | | she | ليست |  ليس also puts its predicate in the accusative: البيت ليس كبيراً (the house is not big). The other tenses have their own negators — لم for the past, لن for the future.

ما (what, before a noun: ما اسمك؟), ماذا (what, before a verb: ماذا تفعل؟), من (who), أين (where), متى (when), كيف (how), لماذا (why) — and هل, which turns any statement into a yes/no question: هل تدرس العربية؟ (Do you study Arabic?). Question word first, sentence unchanged after it.

The past tense (al-māḍī) starts from the bare 3rd-person masculine form — دَرَسَ darasa 'he studied' — and adds a subject suffix: -at (she, دَرَسَتْ), -nā (we, دَرَسْنا), -tum (you pl., دَرَسْتُم), -ū (they, دَرَسوا).  The 'I' and singular 'you' forms add only a final short vowel (دَرَسْتُ darastu, دَرَسْتَ darasta), so they look identical unvowelled. Unlike the present, the past has no subject prefix.

The future prefixes the present-tense verb with سـ (sa-, attached) for the near future or سوف (sawfa, separate) for a more distant or emphatic future: سَيَكْتُب sa-yaktub 'he will write', سوف أذهب sawfa adhhab 'I will go'. Negate the future with لن + subjunctive, not with these particles.

The sound masculine plural leaves the singular whole and adds `ـون` (-ūn) in the subject case, `ـين` (-īn) everywhere else: مُعَلِّم → مُعَلِّمون, رأيتُ المُعَلِّمين. It is mostly for male humans.  The sound feminine plural replaces ة with `ـات` (-āt): مُعَلِّمة → مُعَلِّمات. It also covers many non-human nouns — سيّارات cars, مجلّات magazines — and unlike the masculine it is written the same in every case.  A noun that takes neither ending has a broken plural instead.

Most Arabic nouns pluralize by reshaping the word around the root rather than adding a suffix — the 'broken' plural.  The patterns are fixed and recur:  | singular | plural | romanisation | | --- | --- | --- | | كِتاب | كُتُب | kitāb → kutub | | وَلَد | أَوْلاد | walad → awlād | | بَيْت | بُيوت | bayt → buyūt | | قَلَم | أَقْلام | qalam → aqlām | | رَجُل | رِجال | rajul → rijāl | | مَدينة | مُدُن | madīna → mudun |  You still memorize the plural with each noun, but the shapes come back: وَلَد and قَلَم take the same one.

Arabic has a distinct form for exactly two: `ـان` (-ān) in the subject case, `ـين` (-ayn) everywhere else.  | singular | subject case | other cases | | --- | --- | --- | | كِتاب | كِتابان | كِتابَيْن | | طالِب | طالِبان | طالِبَيْن | | سيّارة | سيّارَتان | سيّارَتَيْن |  A feminine ة opens to ت before the ending: سيّارة → سيّارَتان.  Verbs and adjectives agree in the dual too: كِتابان جديدان.

Prepositions (ḥurūf al-jarr) put the following noun in the genitive (-i / -in).  | preposition | romanisation | meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | في | fī | in | | على | ʿalā | on | | مِن | min | from | | إلى | ilā | to | | عن | ʿan | about | | مع | maʿa | with | | بـ | bi- | with, by | | لـ | li- | for, to |  The last two are written onto the word that follows: بالقلم 'with the pen', للمدرسة 'to the school'.  Many verbs pair with a fixed preposition: تحدّث عن 'talk about', ذهب إلى 'go to'.

The comparative uses the pattern **أَفْعَل** (afʿal) from the adjective's root, invariable for gender, followed by مِن 'than': كبير → أَكْبَر مِن 'bigger than'.  Two root shapes contract — a doubled root writes its twin letters together, a final weak letter becomes ى: مُهِمّ → أَهَمّ 'more important', ذَكِيّ → أَذْكى 'cleverer'.  The same form becomes a superlative when it's made definite or heads an iḍāfa: الأَكْبَر / أَكْبَر مدينة 'the biggest / the biggest city'.

A verbless sentence is put in the past with **كان** kāna. It keeps the subject nominative but makes the predicate — its khabar — accusative: الطقسُ جميلٌ → كان الطقسُ جميلاً 'the weather was nice'.  | subject | form | | --- | --- | | هو | كان | | هي | كانت | | هم | كانوا |  كان always agrees with its subject in gender, but in number only when the subject is a pronoun or stands ahead of it: هم كانوا متعبين, الطلابُ كانوا متعبين — with the verb first it stays singular, كان الطلابُ متعبين.

The object of a verb can attach to it as a suffix instead of standing as a separate word. With رأى raʾā 'he saw':  | object | suffix | verb | | --- | --- | --- | | me | ـني | رآني raʾānī | | you (m.) | ـك | رآك raʾāka | | him | ـه | رآه raʾāhu | | her | ـها | رآها raʾāhā | | them | ـهم | رآهم raʾāhum |  The same suffixes mark possession on a noun and follow a preposition, with one change: 'me' is ـي there (كتابي 'my book', لي 'for me') but ـني on a verb.

From 3 to 10 the counted noun is a plural in the genitive, and the number carries the OPPOSITE gender to it — polarity:  | gender of the singular | number | example | | --- | --- | --- | | masculine | ثلاثة | ثلاثة كُتُب thalāthat kutub | | feminine | ثلاث | ثلاث بنات thalāth banāt |  So the ة sits on the number when the thing counted is masculine, and comes off when it is feminine.  Read the gender off the singular, not off the plural: بِنت is feminine, so ثلاث بنات; إصبع is feminine too, so خمس أصابع.

The subjunctive follows أَنْ 'that', لَنْ 'will not', and حَتّى, كَيْ or لِـ 'so that, in order to'. The verb's final ُ becomes َ: يَكْتُبُ → أن يَكْتُبَ.  Five forms end in ن instead, and that ن drops:  | person | indicative | subjunctive | | --- | --- | --- | | هما | يَكْتُبانِ | يَكْتُبا | | أنتما | تَكْتُبانِ | تَكْتُبا | | هم | يَكْتُبونَ | يَكْتُبوا | | أنتم | تَكْتُبونَ | تَكْتُبوا | | أنتِ | تَكْتُبينَ | تَكْتُبي |  The feminine plural يَكْتُبْنَ is not one of them: its ن is the subject pronoun and never drops.  لَنْ is the standard future negation.

**لَمْ** + the jussive negates the past: لَمْ يَذْهَبْ 'he did not go' — a present-tense form with past meaning.  In the jussive the final ُ becomes sukūn ْ, and the same five forms that lose their ن in the subjunctive lose it here too: لم يَذهَبوا, لم تَذهَبي.  لِـ + the jussive gives a third-person command: لِيَذْهَبْ 'let him go'.

إِنَّ and her 'sisters' begin a nominal sentence and put its subject in the accusative: البيتُ كبيرٌ → إنَّ البيتَ كبيرٌ.  | particle | meaning | | --- | --- | | إِنَّ | indeed | | أَنَّ | that | | لَكِنَّ | but | | لِأَنَّ | because | | كَأَنَّ | as if | | لَعَلَّ | perhaps | | لَيْتَ | if only |  The predicate stays nominative.

The command is built from the jussive: drop the present prefix, and where that leaves a cluster, put a helping alif in front — يَكْتُبُ → اُكْتُبْ 'write!'. The alif is vowelled u when the stem vowel is u, i otherwise: اُكْتُبْ, but اِجْلِسْ and اِفْتَحْ.  | addressee | imperative | | --- | --- | | a man | اُكْتُبْ | | a woman | اُكْتُبي | | a group of men | اُكْتُبوا | | a group of women | اُكْتُبْنَ |  A few everyday verbs are irregular and take no helping alif: تَعالَ / تَعالي 'come'.  Negative commands use لا + jussive: لا تَكْتُبْ 'don't write'.

The maṣdar names the action itself — English 'reading', 'the study of', 'to travel'.  A Form I maṣdar is learned with the verb: قَرَأ → قِراءة (reading), دَرَسَ → دِراسة (study), طَبَخَ → طَبْخ (cooking).  The derived forms are predictable:  | form | maṣdar pattern | example | | --- | --- | --- | | II | تَفْعيل | دَرَّسَ → تَدْريس | | III | مُفاعَلة | سافَرَ → مُسافَرة | | V | تَفَعُّل | تَأَمَّلَ → تَأَمُّل | | X | اِسْتِفْعال | اِسْتَيْقَظَ → اِسْتيقاظ |  Beside مُسافَرة, سَفَر is the everyday word for the travelling itself.  The maṣdar behaves as an ordinary noun (takes ال, iḍāfa, cases) and often replaces an 'أن + verb' clause.

The active participle (ism al-fāʿil) names the doer — كَتَبَ → كاتِب 'writer/writing', on the pattern **فاعِل** for form-I verbs.  The passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl) names the thing acted upon — كُتِبَ → مَكْتوب 'written', on the pattern **مَفْعول**.  Both work as nouns or adjectives and agree in gender and number, the feminine in ـة: كاتِبة، مَكْتوبة.  In a hollow root the middle و or ي surfaces as hamza: نامَ → نائِم 'sleeping', باعَ → بائِع 'seller'.

A definite noun takes a relative pronoun agreeing with it in gender and number — الرجلُ الَّذي جاء 'the man who came'.  | Gender and number | Pronoun | | --- | --- | | m. sg. | الَّذي | | f. sg. | الَّتي | | m. pl. | الَّذينَ | | f. pl. | اللَّاتي | | m. dual | اللَّذانِ | | f. dual | اللَّتانِ |  Only the duals change for case: اللَّذَيْنِ، اللَّتَيْنِ.  The clause carries a resumptive pronoun whenever the noun is not the subject of that clause: الكتابُ الَّذي قرأتُهُ 'the book that I read', with the ـهُ that English drops. Where the noun is the subject, none appears — الَّذي جاء. After an indefinite noun no relative pronoun is used at all: رجلٌ جاء 'a man who came'.

The passive changes the verb's vowels, not its letters: past كَتَبَ → كُتِبَ kutiba 'was written'; present يَكْتُب → يُكْتَب yuktab 'is written'.  The doer is dropped and the object becomes the subject (nominative).  In hollow verbs the change is visible: قال qāla 'said' → قيل qīla 'was said', باع → بيع bīʿa 'was sold'.

Beyond the base (form I), roots take augmented patterns with new meaning.  - Form II فَعَّل doubles the middle root letter and makes the verb causative or intensive: دَرَسَ 'study' → دَرَّسَ 'teach'. - Form III فاعَل adds an alif after the first root letter and aims the action at someone: كَتَبَ 'write' → كاتَبَ 'correspond with'. - Form IV أَفْعَل prefixes أ and is causative: خَرَجَ 'go out' → أَخْرَجَ 'take out, produce'.  All three take a u vowel on the present prefix: يُدَرِّس، يُكاتِب، يُخْرِج.

text: Each of the higher forms rebuilds the root with a prefix or an infix.  - Form V تَفَعَّل is the reflexive of II: عَلَّم 'teach' → تَعَلَّم 'learn (for oneself)'. - Form VI تَفاعَل is the reciprocal of III: كاتَبَ 'correspond with' → تَكاتَبَ 'write to each other'. - Form VII اِنْفَعَل is passive or resultative: كَسَر 'break' → اِنْكَسَر 'break (intr.)'. - Form VIII اِفْتَعَل infixes ت and is often reflexive or mutual: جَمَع 'gather' → اِجْتَمَع 'gather, meet'. - Form X اِسْتَفْعَل means seek or consider: خَدَم 'serve' → اِسْتَخْدَم 'use', غَفَر 'forgive' → اِسْتَغْفَر 'ask forgiveness'.  Form IX اِفْعَلَّ is rare and confined to colours and defects: اِحْمَرَّ 'turn red'.
stratum: point:Derived verb forms V–X (تفعّل، انفعل، افتعل، استفعل)

text: - إذا + past states a likely future condition, and the answer clause is past in form too though its sense is future: إذا دَرَسْتَ نَجَحْتَ 'if you study, you'll pass'. - إِنْ + jussive is the formal equivalent: إن تَدْرُسْ تَنْجَحْ. - لَوْ + past is counterfactual — it didn't happen — and its answer clause opens with لـ: لَوْ دَرَسْتَ لَنَجَحْتَ 'had you studied, you'd have passed'.  That لـ drops when the answer clause is negative: لَوْ دَرَسْتَ ما رَسَبْتَ 'had you studied, you would not have failed'.

The ḥāl is an accusative word describing the subject's or object's state while the main action happens — English '…ing' or 'while…': جاء الولدُ راكِضًا 'the boy came running', شَرِبْتُ القهوةَ ساخِنةً 'I drank the coffee hot'.  It is indefinite and agrees with its owner in gender and number, so the accusative surfaces as a different ending on each shape:  | Owner | Ending | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | m. sg. | ـًا | راكِضًا | | f. sg. | ـةً | ساخِنةً | | m. pl. | ـينَ | مُسْرِعينَ | | f. pl. | ـاتٍ | مُسْرِعاتٍ |

The tamyīz is an accusative noun that specifies what a vague amount or comparison refers to — English 'in…', 'of…', '…-wise'. It is singular, indefinite and accusative, and it follows three things:  - a verb of filling or increase: اِمْتَلأَ الكوبُ ماءً 'the cup filled with water', اِزْدادَ الطالبُ عِلمًا 'the student grew in knowledge' - a comparative: أنتَ أكثرُ مِنّي مالًا 'you are richer than me in money' - a measure or a number: اِشْتَرَيْتُ رِطْلًا عِنَبًا 'I bought a pound of grapes', عِشْرونَ كِتابًا 'twenty books'

Roots containing و or ي behave irregularly.  - Assimilated (مثال, initial و): the و drops in the present — وَصَلَ 'arrive' → يَصِل. - Hollow (أجوف, middle و/ي): قالَ → يَقول. The long vowel shortens in the jussive and the command — قُلْ — and before a consonant ending in the past: عادَ → عُدْتُ 'I returned'. - Defective (ناقص, final و/ي): دَعا → يَدْعو, مَشى → يَمْشي, and the weak letter drops in the jussive: لم يَدْعُ، لم يَمْشِ.

إلّا excludes one item from a whole: جاء الطلابُ إلّا واحِدًا 'the students came except one' — after a full affirmative sentence the excepted noun is accusative. In a negative sentence it takes the case its own role demands: ما نَجَحَ إلّا طالِبٌ 'no one passed but a student', where طالِبٌ is the subject of the verb.  غَيْر and سِوى do the same job as nouns: what follows them is genitive, and they themselves take the case the excepted noun would have had after إلّا — جاء الطلابُ غَيْرَ واحِدٍ. سِوى never shows its ending.

Address someone with يا:  - يا + a single noun: يا طالِبُ 'O student' — the noun takes a nominative-like ending and no tanwīn. - يا أيُّها + a masculine noun with الـ: يا أيُّها الناسُ 'O people'. - يا أيَّتُها + a feminine noun with الـ: يا أيَّتُها السيّدةُ 'O madam'.  For strong emphasis the energetic نون attaches to the verb after the لـ of an oath: لأَكْتُبَنَّ 'I shall certainly write', واللهِ لأَنجَحَنَّ 'by God, I will surely succeed'.

Arabic's default verb-first order can be reordered for emphasis by fronting (taqdīm): putting the object or a prepositional phrase first highlights it — إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ 'You alone we worship', في البيتِ رجلٌ 'in the house is a man'. A fronted object pronoun appears in its إيّا- form, because a suffixed pronoun cannot stand at the head of the sentence.  Restriction ('only') is expressed with إِنَّما or with ما … إلّا: إِنَّما المؤمنونَ إخوةٌ 'the believers are but brothers', ما نَجَحَ إلّا المُجتَهِدُ 'none succeeded but the diligent'.

Elevated Arabic organizes discourse with fixed devices.  - أمّا … فـ picks out a topic and comments on it: أمّا الطُّلابُ فَمُجْتَهِدونَ 'as for the students, they are diligent'. The فـ is obligatory. - قَدْ + past asserts that the action definitely happened: قد وَصَلَ 'he has indeed arrived'. لَقَدْ intensifies it. - قَدْ + present means 'may' or 'sometimes': قد يُخْطِئُ الإنسانُ 'a person sometimes errs'.
